I am a 49-year-old woman from Quzhou County. I have farmed this land since I was young, just like my mother and grandmother before me. I never went to school, but I know this soil and this climate with my own two hands.

This year, I will plant **winter wheat** on about 4 mu of my land, and after we harvest it in early June, I will sow **summer maize** on the same 4 mu. That is the rotation everyone here follows — it is the only way to get two crops from one piece of land in a single year. I do not grow cotton anymore because the labor is too heavy for me now, and the wheat-maize rotation gives steadier income.

For the wheat, I will use the improved seeds from the government supply store. They yield better than the old varieties. I will rotary-till the field before sowing in October, put down about 100 jin of compound fertilizer as basal, and then top-dress with urea or ammonium bicarbonate when the wheat greens up in spring. I will irrigate three times — once at sowing, once at green-up, and once at grain-filling — because the rain here is never enough. I will also spray pesticides four or five times when I see insects or when the neighbors start spraying, and I apply herbicide once to control weeds.

For the maize, I will buy hybrid seed, usually Denghai or Nongda brands, because everyone says they are high-yielding. After the wheat comes out in June, I will sow the maize directly without extra tillage — no-tillage saves time and diesel. I will put down compound fertilizer at sowing and irrigate twice during the summer if it gets dry. I spray insecticide and herbicide a few times, but maize is hardier than wheat so I do not fuss over it as much.

I expect my wheat to yield around 580 kg per mu and the maize around 525 kg per mu, which is about what I usually get in a normal year.
